To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a gene-diet interaction score (GDIS) was derived from 2 genes (PPARγ2 and FABP2) and 2 nutrients (saturated and polyunsaturated fat), and this GDIS predicted the response to dietary fat on body weight, body mass index, waist circumference, body fat percentage and fat mass in postmenopausal women in the Women's health Initiative.
a gene-diet interaction score based on SNPs in FTO, MC4R, SH2B1, and TMEM18 genes, as well as a score based on the SNPs in FADS2 and FADS1 genes, can predict response to a high-fat diet.
a gene-diet interaction (GDI)-based score predicts response to a high-fat diet (HFD) in the Women's Healthy Initiative (WHI).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the relationship between diet and health, with the aim of identifying dietary patterns that can reduce the risk of disease and promote good health.
the role of diet in the prevention of chronic disease, with particular reference to the prevention of cardiovascular disease, cancer and diabetes.
the development of a novel, noninvasive, in vivo, real-time, optical imaging method to detect early stage cancer in the oral cavity, and in the head and neck regions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results from the WHI trial of dietary fat and breast cancer are inconclusive.
a high intake of dietary fat is not related to the risk of breast cancer.
a diet low in fat and saturated fat, high in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, with an adequate intake of dietary fiber and moderate in alcohol, is associated with a reduced risk for CHD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a diet high in fat is bad for you, but that a diet rich in fat from fish, nuts and olive oil is good for you, and a diet low in fat from red meat, processed meat and dairy products is bad for you.
a gene-diet interaction based score predicts response to fat in the WHI.
the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) Dietary Modification trial (WHI-DM) was a randomized trial of dietary intervention that did not reduce risk for breast cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there are genetic differences between people in the way they process and respond to dietary fat and that this genetic difference may be a factor in explaining why some people respond to low-fat diets and others do not.
the genetic risk score is a better predictor of the response to dietary fat than any individual SNP.
the gene-diet interaction score is a better predictor of weight change in response to dietary fat compared to the gene-diet score or the gene-diet-gene score.
